c.tagline: The Blue City beneath a mighty desert fort, gateway to the Thar.

taxi.fareNote: Yellow-and-green auto-rickshaws are the everyday ride but are unmetered, so agree the fare before setting off or use Uber/Ola for a fixed price. UPI apps (PhonePe, Google Pay) are widely accepted for payment.

emergency.note: 112 is India's unified emergency number connecting to police, fire and ambulance; 100 reaches police and 108 the ambulance service directly.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Touts and commission scams around the fort and markets

hood_desc: The photogenic tangle of indigo-washed old houses climbing the hill below Mehrangarh Fort; narrow, largely car-free lanes, hidden guesthouses and rooftop cafes with fort views make this the atmospheric first-timer base of the 'Blue City'.

The commercial heart around the landmark Ghanta Ghar (Clock Tower) and the horseshoe-shaped Sardar Market, packed with spice stalls, textiles and sweets and steps from the Toorji Ka Jhalra stepwell; best for shopping, street food and staying in the thick of old-town life.

A greener, upscale district southeast of the center holding the grand Umaid Bhawan Palace and several heritage hotels; suits travelers wanting palace-grade luxury, gardens and calm within a short drive of the sights.

A modern commercial and residential quarter with the widest choice of mid-range hotels, banks, cafes and restaurants along a grid of busy streets; a practical, well-connected base for those who prefer new-town convenience.

A quieter residential neighbourhood on the city's outskirts toward the airport, with local markets and a handful of resort-style and business hotels; suits longer stays and travelers wanting a calmer base away from the crowds.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water only.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 9:00 PM; auto-rickshaws and app cabs run later into the night.
transit.note: Jodhpur has no metro; getting around means city buses, ubiquitous yellow-and-green auto-rickshaws and app cabs (Uber/Ola). The Blue City's old-town lanes are best explored on foot.
transit.pay: Pay bus and auto fares in cash; autos are unmetered, so agree the fare first or use an app. UPI (PhonePe/Google Pay) is widely accepted.

bus: RSRTC intercity buses to Jaipur, Udaipur, Jaisalmer and Delhi
train: Indian Railways (Jodhpur Junction) to Delhi, Jaipur, Jaisalmer, Ahmedabad and Mumbai

transit.m: Auto-rickshaw to the city center (~15-20 min)
Uber/Ola or prepaid taxi to the center (15 min)

tip.r: Around 10% at restaurants (check first for a service charge); small notes for hotel staff, drivers and guides are appreciated.

food.name: Mirchi bada
food.desc: A whole mild green chilli stuffed with spiced potato, dipped in gram-flour batter and deep-fried. Jodhpur's own snack, eaten with chutney.

places.name: Shahi Samosa
places.note: Clock Tower-area landmark that fries mirchi bada and samosa non-stop all day.

places.name: Janta Sweet Home
places.note: Long-running sweet house famous for mirchi bada, kachori and ghevar.

places.name: Chand Vilas Namkeen
places.note: Local name for consistently good namkeen and a well-made mirchi bada.

food.name: Pyaaz kachori
food.desc: Flaky fried pastry packed with spiced onion masala, cracked open and topped with tamarind chutney. Standard Rajasthani breakfast fuel.

places.name: Janta Sweet Home
places.note: Reliable all-day kachori counter in the middle of the old-city shopping street.

places.name: Shahi Samosa

places.name: Jodhpur Sweets House
places.note: Newer-town sweet shop that locals rate for kachori and namkeen.

food.name: Mawa kachori
food.desc: Sweet kachori stuffed with khoya, nuts and cardamom, deep-fried and soaked in sugar syrup. The dessert Jodhpur is known for nationally.

places.name: Janta Sweet Home
places.note: Probably the most-cited address in the city for mawa kachori.

places.name: Ghas Mandi sweet shops
places.note: Old-city lane long regarded by locals as the source of the best mawa kachori.

places.name: Jodhpur Sweets House
places.note: Handy stop for boxed mithai and mawa kachori to take away.

food.name: Laal maas
food.desc: Fiery Rajasthani mutton curry built on Mathania red chillies and yoghurt, hunting food turned royal-kitchen classic. Eat with bajra roti.

places.name: On The Rocks

places.name: Indique

places.name: Jhankar Choti Haveli

places.name: Gypsy Dining Hall
places.note: Unlimited Rajasthani thali where ker sangri arrives with a dozen other dishes.

places.name: Jhankar Choti Haveli
places.note: Traditional Marwari vegetarian plates in a shaded old-city courtyard.

places.name: Indique

food.name: Dal baati churma
food.desc: Baked wheat balls cracked open over ghee, dunked in five-lentil dal and finished with sweet crumbled churma. Rajasthan on one plate.

places.name: Gypsy Dining Hall
places.note: Thali institution where the servers keep refilling until you surrender.

places.name: Jhankar Choti Haveli

places.name: On The Rocks
places.note: Comfortable garden setting for the full Rajasthani spread in the evening.

food.name: Makhaniya lassi
food.desc: Jodhpur's saffron-and-cardamom lassi, so thick with butter and cream it is eaten with a spoon and topped with pistachio.

landmarks: Mehrangarh Fort
One of India's mightiest citadels rears 120 meters above the Blue City on sheer cliffs, sheltering opulent palaces, latticed courtyards and a superb museum.
Jaswant Thada
A luminous white-marble cenotaph of Maharaja Jaswant Singh II, its carved lattice screens glow translucent at sunrise beside a tranquil lake below Mehrangarh.
Umaid Bhawan Palace
One of the world's largest private residences, this golden-sandstone Art Deco palace houses the royal family, a Taj hotel and a vintage-car museum.
Ghanta Ghar (Clock Tower) and Sardar Market
Jodhpur's beloved Victorian-era clock tower anchors a chaotic bazaar of spice pyramids, bangles, textiles and the city's famous makhania lassi stalls.
Toorji Ka Jhalra (Stepwell)
An 18th-century stepwell of rose-red sandstone plunging in geometric flights, restored into Jodhpur's most photogenic gathering spot ringed by cafés.
Blue City Old Town (Navchokiya)
A maze of indigo-washed havelis and temple-studded lanes beneath the fort, where every rooftop frames the iconic blue panorama photographers chase.
Mandore Gardens
The ancient Marwar capital's rock-terraced gardens shelter soaring red-sandstone royal cenotaphs, a hall of folk heroes and troops of langur monkeys.
Rao Jodha Desert Rock Park
A 70-hectare restored desert ecosystem beneath Mehrangarh's walls, with volcanic-rock trails winding through native flora to dramatic fort viewpoints.
Kaylana Lake
An artificial lake west of the city framed by rocky Aravalli outcrops, beloved for fiery sunsets and winter flamingos and migratory birds.
Osian Temples
An oasis town north of Jodhpur, dubbed the Khajuraho of Rajasthan for its intricately sculpted 8th-to-11th-century Jain and Hindu temples and dunes.

train.note: No international trains. Jodhpur Junction sits below the fort in the middle of town, with overnight trains to Delhi and Jaipur and services west to Jaisalmer (about 6 hours) - the Jaisalmer overnight is the classic desert run. Book on IRCTC 60 days ahead, especially in the cool October-March season.

bus.note: No international coaches. RSRTC (https://rsrtconline.rajasthan.gov.in/) buses leave the Raika Bagh and central bus stands for Jaisalmer, Udaipur, Jaipur and Ahmedabad, and private sleepers are bookable through redBus (https://www.redbus.in/). The Jaisalmer bus takes about 5 hours against the train's 6.

ferry.note: Jodhpur sits on the edge of the Thar Desert with no navigable water, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Bishnoi Villages
half.blurb: Rural Bishnoi communities known for wildlife conservation and blackbuck sightings on jeep safaris outside Jodhpur.

full.name: Ranakpur Jain Temple
full.blurb: An elaborately carved marble Jain temple complex with over 1,400 pillars, about three hours from Jodhpur.

full.name: Kumbhalgarh Fort
full.blurb: A hilltop fortress with one of the longest continuous walls in the world, roughly three hours from Jodhpur.
